rationale: Start with a broad, mid-temperature scouting gradient to elute all 8 compounds and map the full elution window without risking truncation. This should reveal whether peaks are compressed early, late, or across the gradient so later runs can narrow the window and tune slope.

All peaks eluted between about phi_e 0.21 and 0.44, so the first run used a much wider gradient window than needed. Narrowing the window around the observed elution region at the same slope duration should improve selectivity for the unresolved middle pair while keeping all compounds within the gradient and still under 10 minutes.

Hold the same focused phi window and double tG to test whether the critical pairs, especially (4,5), respond to shallower gradient slope. If resolution improves substantially, slope is the main lever; if not, we will know to pivot to temperature or phi-window shifts for selectivity.

The unresolved pair improved with shallower slope, but not enough, so selectivity likely matters too. Lowering temperature at the better 20 min method probes whether the critical pair can be separated by a temperature-induced selectivity shift without incurring the time penalty seen at 40 min.

We already have full resolution with the last peak under 10 min, so the only remaining objective is to shorten the method until a pair drops below R = 1.5. Reducing tG by one step while keeping the successful window and temperature is the cleanest first optimization.

The 18 min run still has full resolution and the limiting pair is now only modestly above threshold, so another 2 min reduction directly tests whether we can shorten further while staying at CRF 1.000. This is the fastest remaining one-variable move around the current optimum.

Since 16 min was too steep mainly for pair (3,4), keep the successful 18 min slope neighborhood but slightly narrow the upper end of the gradient window to spend more gradient around the elution region of the later peaks. This may preserve full resolution while trimming retention a bit further or improving margin on the critical pair.

Lowering phi1 to 0.65 kept full resolution but lengthened the run, so try the opposite direction: a slightly higher phi1 at the proven 18 min, 25 C condition. This should pull the late peaks earlier while likely retaining enough margin on the critical (3,4) pair to stay fully resolved.

The limiting pair is sensitive to gradient steepness/window, and the first peak is still safely retained, so lowering phi0 by one step should shift more of the early-middle region into a shallower effective gradient without pushing t_last past 10 min. This tests whether we can keep full resolution at 18 min while potentially preserving or improving runtime.

At 18 min and 25 C we are exactly at the full-resolution boundary, while 16 min failed because pair (3,4) lost resolution. A small temperature increase may shorten the run while preserving enough selectivity to keep that pair at or above R = 1.5, potentially giving a faster fully resolved method.

At 30 C, 18 min became slightly too aggressive, but the limiting pair moved late in the chromatogram, suggesting the temperature is usable if the slope is softened a bit. Increasing tG to 20 min tests whether we can regain full resolution at 30 C while keeping the run faster than the 20 min, 25 C baseline.

The 18 min, 0.65 endpoint run had extra resolution margin but was a bit slower than 18 min, 0.70; combining that narrower window with a shorter 16 min gradient may land between the successful 18 min and failed 16 min cases. This specifically tests whether we can recover a fully resolved faster method by using the more favorable selectivity window.

The 0.65 window appears to give better selectivity margin than 0.70, and at 16 min it still fully resolves all peaks with the same limiting pair at R 1.61. Reducing to 14 min is the next direct step to locate the shortest fully resolved method in this more favorable window.

At 0.65/16 min we are fully resolved but right near the boundary, while 0.65/14 min is too steep. Lowering phi1 one more step at 16 min should further flatten the effective gradient over the critical elution region and may open extra margin on pair (3,4), potentially enabling a later attempt at a shorter fully resolved run.

The 0.60 endpoint at 16 min increased resolution margin on the critical pair compared with 0.65/16, so it is the best platform to test one more shortening step. Running 14 min here checks whether that extra selectivity margin is enough to keep all pairs at or above R = 1.5 while gaining speed.

The 14 min method at phi1 0.60 still gives full resolution with the limiting pair at R 1.61, so one more 2 min reduction is the next boundary test for the shortest fully resolved method. This directly checks whether we can improve speed further before pair (3,4) falls below threshold.

Since 12 min at 0.25–0.60 was too steep for pair (3,4), try narrowing the window from the low end while keeping the successful 14 min duration. Raising phi0 should compress the early dead space and may shift gradient focus toward the critical middle region, potentially opening a path to a shorter fully resolved method if selectivity changes favorably.

Raising phi0 severely collapsed the critical pair, so keep phi0 at 0.25 and instead lower phi1 by one step from the successful 0.25–0.60/14 min method. This narrows the gradient further while preserving the favorable low-end conditions, testing whether we can gain enough selectivity margin on pair (3,4) to support faster optimization.

The 0.25–0.55, 14 min method has the largest margin yet on the limiting pair while still staying under 10 min, so it is the best candidate for another shortening test. Dropping to 12 min checks whether that added selectivity margin is enough to produce a faster fully resolved method.

The 12 min run at 0.25–0.55 still fully resolves all compounds with the limiting pair at R 1.61, so this is now the strongest candidate for one final shortening step. Testing 10 min directly identifies whether we can move below the current boundary while keeping CRF at 1.000.

At 12 min, the 0.25–0.55 window is right on the full-resolution boundary, and lowering phi1 has consistently improved margin on the critical pair at the cost of some retention. Testing 0.25–0.50 at 12 min asks whether we can keep full resolution with a different, slightly narrower window that might still remain under the 10 min last-peak limit.

The 0.25–0.50 window at 12 min gives full resolution with the largest margin on the critical pair seen near this speed, though t_last is close to 10 min. Reducing to 10 min is the key boundary test to see whether this narrower window can deliver a shorter fully resolved method than our current 12 min winner.

At 10 min, 0.25–0.50 still gives full resolution with useful margin on the limiting pair, so lowering phi1 one more step is the best remaining way to search for an even shorter effective window without changing temperature or phi0. This tests whether extra selectivity from a narrower window can support the shortest robust fully resolved method.

The 0.25–0.50, 10 min method is currently the shortest fully resolved condition, so with two injections left the highest-value test is one more reduction in tG at the same favorable window. This will determine whether an even shorter fully resolved method exists or confirm 10 min as the practical boundary.

A lower phi1 improved the critical pair but pushed the last peak just beyond 10 min at 10 min tG; lengthening to 12 min while keeping the narrower window tests whether this selectivity-favored condition can remain fully resolved and stay at or just under the 10 min limit. It is the best remaining untried point near the current optimum.
